properties.description:
flo2 F24, on Anthony's word of 2026-09-22 ("go with F24 next"). `describe_schema` served the node TYPES and not the rules that tell them apart, so a consumer generating an extraction prompt from the schema got type names and nothing that separates them — and a numeric prohibition was filed as a Requirement on a live site.

⭐ THE WORK TURNED OUT TO BE ORDERED, NOT SINGLE. Lifting the routing table into data exposed that the table CONTRADICTED ITSELF: row 1 routed "it must never…" to Requirement while row 7 routed "we must never…" to Constraint saying "Not a Requirement", so the rule turned on a pronoun and flo2's sentence matched the wrong row. Serving it unchanged would have propagated a wrong rule to every consumer at once. The table was corrected first, then served.

WHAT LANDS: `discrimination` per node type in the schema (cue phrases in a person's own words, the neighbouring type and why they differ, a worked counter-example), carried through `NodeTypeSpec` so `describe_schema` serves it for free; eight routed types filled in; the routing table corrected; and `tools/check_discrimination_rules.py` wired into CI as the gate that keeps the two records one contract.

NOT IN THIS EPOCH, and separable: `prohibition_in_prose`'s six phrasings are all built on MUST or ALLOWED/FORBIDDEN and cover no CAN — "can never", "cannot", "may not", "shall not" all miss. That is the OTHER half of F24 and has a different cause from the one this epoch fixes.
properties.name: The schema serves the rules that tell the types apart — and the rules were wrong first (2026-09-22)
